extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of medieval/Crusades history
extracted.subtask_description: Narrative account of the Crusades (roughly 1095–1229) analysing political, military and religious causes and consequences, with focus on factors determining success or failure of individual Crusades (Third, Fourth, Fifth, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of Egypt as decisive factor
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the future, events hinged on the situation of affairs in Egypt, and in Egypt the fate of the kingdom of Jerusalem was finally decided.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly treats possession and influence in Egypt as the strategic pivot: rivalries in Egypt (Shirkuh/Shirguh vs. Amalric), Saladin's rise to sole ruler of Egypt (1171) and the eventual political/unity consequences determine the long-term fate of the Latin kingdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity or disunion of Muslim powers vs Franks
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus the Shiite caliphate became extinct ... and the long-disunited Mahommedans at last faced the Christians as a solid body.”; “If a religious union had been effected between Egypt and northern Syria, political disunion still remained; and the Franks were safe as long as it lasted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and religious unification among Muslim polities greatly increases the danger to Crusader states; conversely, Muslim disunion gives the Franks breathing space. Evaluations of threat and timing hinge on whether opponents are united.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership, command unity and political cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Crusade had failed—failed because a leaderless army, torn by political dissensions and fighting on a foreign soil, could not succeed against forces united by religious zeal under the banner of a leader like Saladin.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal divisions between monarchs, competing claimants and factional disputes (e.g., Philip vs. Richard, Guy vs. Conrad) undermine military effectiveness and are cited as direct causes of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal (spiritual) direction versus lay (secular) leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The Third Crusade “does not spring from the papacy ... it springs from the lay power”; later, “the crusading movement was being lost to the papacy, and becoming part of the demesne of the secular state.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that papal/spiritual leadership preserves the religious intent and 'elan' of a Crusade, while lay/secular direction tends to politicize and corrupt objectives—this is used as a criterion for judging the character and likely outcome of Crusading efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing and taxation as a necessary basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to the Saladin tithe: taxation “provided a necessary financial basis for military operations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective funding (taxation schemes, levies) is presented as a necessary precondition for mounting large-scale expeditions; taxation also influenced recruitment (pushing people to take the cross to avoid the tithe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding diversion to political/commercial aims (preventing strategic diversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourth Crusade was diverted to Constantinople: “The Crusade lost its _elan_ when it became a move in a political game.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversion of Crusading expeditions to secular or commercial ends (e.g., Venetian cupidity, Hohenstaufen objectives) is judged detrimental: it changes objectives, drains resources from the Holy Land, and undermines moral legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime logistics and choice of route (naval capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: With Syria in Mahommedan hands, “the attack on Egypt must necessarily be directed by sea; and thus the Crusade ... becomes ... a maritime enterprise.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naval transport, agreements with maritime powers (e.g., Venice), and the ability to conduct seaborne operations are treated as crucial practical criteria when the strategic objective requires access by sea; contractual/logistical arrangements (costs, concessions) materially shape outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomacy and negotiated settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Richard’s negotiations with Saladin leading to a three-year peace (Sept. 2, 1192) by which certain towns were divided and pilgrims allowed access to the Holy Sepulchre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiation can yield pragmatic concessions and preserve interests even when military objectives fail; diplomatic skill is therefore a criterion for assessing overall success or salvageable outcomes of a Crusade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynastic choices, rule legitimacy and internal succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Sibylla’s marriage to Guy de Lusignan was “destined to be the cause of many dissensions”; coronation “in violation of the promise given to Raymund” produced weak title and inability to control the kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy of rulers, adherence to succession agreements and wise marital alliances are treated as essential for internal stability; poor dynastic decisions produce factionalism and weaken defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting truces and avoiding provocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Raynald’s attack on a caravan in which Saladin’s sister was travelling “thus violating a four years' truce ... meant the ruin of the kingdom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provocations that break truces can trigger powerful reprisals; prudent statesmanship requires honoring truces or risk provoking united and energetic retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morale, religious zeal and home-ground advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Saladin’s army “had the spirit and the fire of the Latin crusaders of 1099. The tables were turned; and fighting on their own soil ... the Mahommedans easily carried the day.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fighting for a perceived holy cause on home soil, with high morale and leadership, is emphasized as a decisive advantage; morale and motive are recurrent criteria in battle outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securing powerful allies and patronage (Byzantine, local rulers)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The patronage of Constantinople ... contributed to some slight extent in maintaining the kingdom ... Baldwin and Amalric both married into the Comnenian house ... Manuel enjoyed the homage of Antioch.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alliances with the Byzantine empire or local powers, and dynastic ties, can materially strengthen the Latin kingdom; loss of key allies (e.g., fall of Damascus) removes vital strategic support.

rubrics_metrics.name: State organization and the use of Crusade for secular aims
rubrics_metrics.description: “The state would take up the name of Crusade in order to cover, and under such cover to achieve, its own objects and ambitions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats the transformation of Crusades into instruments of state policy as an evaluative lens: when Crusades serve secular state ambitions rather than spiritual ends, their nature and effects change (often detrimentally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace at home and economic measures as preconditions of success
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Fourth Lateran (1215) it was resolved that “a truce of God should reign for the next four years, while for the same time all trade with the Levant should cease.” The author notes these as measures which 14th-century pamphleteers unanimously advocate “as the necessary conditions of success.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Securing domestic peace (ceasing internal warfare) and pursuing economic pressure (trade embargoes) against the enemy are presented as strategic prerequisites for a successful, sustained expedition.
